title: Overfitting: memorizing versus learning
hook: A model that aces practice and fails live. How to spot it, and what to do.
inPlainWords: Overfitting is a student who memorizes last year's exam answers. Great on the practice paper, lost on a new question.

useCase.title: A delivery-time model that fails after launch
useCase.story: Your model predicted delivery days perfectly on the data it trained on, but live predictions are off by days. You only have 1,500 past deliveries.

approaches.name: Hold-out exam set
approaches.what: Keep some data hidden until the end.

approaches.name: Cross-validation
approaches.what: Rotate which part is the exam several times, then average the scores.
approaches.greatWhen: Small data where you want a steadier score.
approaches.avoidWhen: Very large data, or data ordered in time.
approaches.example: Five different exams from the same data.

approaches.name: Simplify the model
approaches.what: Limit how much it can memorize, with fewer or shallower rules.
approaches.greatWhen: The model is too flexible for the data you have.
approaches.avoidWhen: The model is already too simple.
approaches.example: Limit trees to a few questions deep.

approaches.name: Get more data
approaches.greatWhen: It is the cheapest cure when possible.

approaches.name: Stop early or add a penalty
approaches.what: Stop training before it starts memorizing, or penalize complexity.
approaches.example: Stop when the exam score stops improving.

approaches.name: Split by time
approaches.what: Train on the past and test on the future.
approaches.example: Train on January to September, test on October.

challenge.question: Practice score 99%, exam score 70%. What is the most sensible first move?

options.why: The practice score only shows memory, not skill.

options.text: Simplify or limit the model, add data if you can, and re-check the exam score
options.why: It attacks the memorizing directly, and the exam score tells you if it worked.
Longer training usually memorizes even more.

options.text: Run cross-validation to confirm the gap is real
options.why: Good for confirming, but it does not fix anything.

bestCase.title: Trust the exam score, and shrink the gap
bestCase.example: The team limits tree depth and adds another year of deliveries. The practice score drops to 82% and the exam score rises to 79%. The gap is small, so live results match what was measured.

worstCase.title: Trusting the practice score
worstCase.example: The model memorized 1,500 deliveries, including quirks like one courier's slow Tuesday. Live, it predicts 2 days for a parcel that takes 6. Customers are given wrong promises.

steps.label: Split by time
steps.goes: Train on January to September, exam on October and November.
steps.goesWrong: There is no exam set. The model is judged on the same parcels it learned from.

steps.label: Train a limited model
steps.goes: Shallow rules leave no room to memorize.

steps.label: Compare the two scores
steps.goes: Practice 82%, exam 79%. The gap is small.

steps.label: Adjust if the gap is big
steps.goes: Simplify the model or add data.

steps.label: Go live and monitor
steps.goes: Track live accuracy against the exam score.

takeaway: Judge a model only on data it has never seen, and watch the gap between practice and exam.
